utterances.text: Well, there would be some commanders who would over-step their limits, their remit, and then they would come to me -- people would come to me and send me their explanations set out in a letter and so on, and I would consult the ministers and would stay the order, for example, issued by the commander of the 124th Brigade of the Croatian Army in this particular instance. And I said that they couldn't send people to the Posavina battle-field. They could go if they were volunteers. Now, Your Honours, you will see that an order is written and people being sent voluntarily, as volunteers, so that's a problem, a problem that would occur when certain members wanted to go as volunteers. They -- the question was: What would happen if that person were killed, what rights the family members had, and unless you provided them with a piece of paper saying that you were sending them there, although these people were volunteers, then he and his family could not enjoy the benefits provided by the Croatian state if something happened to them there. So you have a problem whereby people would go voluntarily and an order would, nonetheless, be written, but if you had an order written without the volunteers, that order would be stayed. And, for example, a general on one occasion was taken to court or, rather, there was an investigation and inquiry undertaken for the fact that he wrote an order, so he had to go through the procedure of being taken to task, and the whole question rested on his unit crossing over the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You made a slip of the tongue. You said he filed a criminal report, where actually you meant to say that he issued an order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and he was taken to task, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This brings us to the next document, which is 3D03091.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have this document dated 16th of September, 1992. It prohibits the 124th HV Brigade from going to the Posavina battle-field. This is a clear document. As far as you know, because this is a very relevant question, by the way, as are all my questions, were they units of the Croatian Army that found themselves in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with all their equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will answer correctly. Pursuant to an order, some units of the Croatian Army went to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina only in the vicinity of Dubrovnik, because Dubrovnik could not have been defended in any different way. The territory is simply too narrow. If you wanted to reach the border, you couldn't, because it is on top of the hill, and if you did only that, they could still keep on pounding Dubrovnik from the border. During the operation to liberate Dubrovnik, the units did cross into the hinterland, and that was the only way to do it. And I believe that that was also permissible, as far as I read the literature and as far as I informed myself about that. The second time it happened was on the 10th of April, 1992, and that was the day when I was appointed commander of South-Western Herzegovina. Pursuant to an order, one battalion, the 4th Battalion of the 4th Guards Brigade, with 160 men, crossed the border in order to cover a gap in the territory between Citluk and Mostar, in order to prevent an expected breakthrough of the Yugoslav People's Army towards Split, and 160 men is an insignificant number. They stayed there for a short while, and as soon as I managed to amass the army, they left. While I was there, as far as I know, it never happened that the Croatian Army crossed the border pursuant to an order. Volunteers did that. In military terms, their number was insignificant. I claim that there were never more than 500 or 600 of them scattered all over the place in a random way. When I became commander down there, and you will see the document - this was on the 24th of July, 1993 - I asked Minister Susak and President Tudjman to take into account the very adverse military situation after the breakthrough of Muslims across Bugojno, that I be provided with at least two battalions of the Croatian Army to be put at my disposal. Of course, they wouldn't allow that. I, as a soldier, requested that, although I knew very well that I would be turned down, that my request would be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, as far as you know, if an HV unit had found themselves in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the internal documents of the said unit would one find any trace of this transport from the Republic of Croatia towards the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? And I'm going to be even clearer than this, because now we don't want to waste any more time. We really have to go to the heart of the matter, so I'll be even more specific. We heard witnesses who spoke about the Heliodrom, and mention was made of the presence of HV units. So you are under oath. Are you telling me that as far as you know, there never was a single HV unit that crossed the border in order to go to a battle-field in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? One couldn't be any clearer than this, could one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, save for the unit with 160 men in 1992, on the 10th of April, who went there to close the gap, in Heliodrom, in its surroundings, there was never a unit of the Croatian Army that would have arrived pursuant to an order as an HV unit. In a situation that I was in, I did request -- I did implore my peers, commanders in Croatia, and I received from the 1st Guards Brigade -- I had some 40 men who came from there, and then a few lads came with whom I had waged a war in Sunja. 500 of them volunteered to come. I did appeal to the volunteers to join me, but I never requested and a request was never approved for a unit of the Croatian Army to be sent. It is true that volunteers, when they came, they would be covered by an order, and this is what instills confusion. He -- they would say, I am going as a volunteer, but I still need a paper. People will get killed. They were ready to get killed, but they were wondering what would happen with their wife, children, and parents. The Croatian government and the Croatian minister of defence were of an opinion that the volunteers would receive their salary and all the other benefits as they would in Croatia, but they were still considered volunteers. And that applied to the Croats in the BiH Army and the Croats in the HV. The same rule applied, and the documents will prove that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Again we have an error in the transcript. On page 53, line 24 and line 25, General Praljak said that this applied to the Croats and Muslims in the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the same rules applied, because both groups went there as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Even before that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General Praljak, we have thousands of documents, and I believe there's one, but I can't remember it's number, you'll forgive me, because it's impossible to keep all the document numbers in mind, all the more so because I had not planned to ask you this. But your reply prompted this, so I quote from memory, but I never make a mistake. I believe that there is one international observer who said that he saw an HV unit pass by, so could it be that he was confused, that he made a mistake? Were there volunteers who went by? How can you account for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, there were some ignorant observers who would see two or three men bearing the insignia of the Croatian Army and they would call them a unit. Second of all, Your Honours, you've heard a witness here who said that he had seen a division of the Croatian Army, and when I asked him how many men, he said, 50. Where? Down there near Metkovic or close to the Croatian border. Third of all, we're going to hear a witness whom I can't mention by name. He is an American who will say precisely how much and to what extent those men erred when they said that they saw the Croatian Army. Another important thing. Despite the fact that General Petkovic and myself provided very clear instructions, saying that when people came from Croatia as volunteers, from the Croatian Army, that they had to remove their original insignia and replace them by the HVO insignia, that was sometimes not done. That's just because some lads wanted to boast for being members of another unit, a glorious unit. Your Honours, I would also sometimes wear the insignia of the Croatian Army because I had two uniforms. While one was in the wash, I wore the other one. And when somebody saw me, they would say, Okay, there is a guy from the Croatian Army, but I simply didn't have anything else to put on. I'm a big man, and it was difficult to find a suitable uniform for me. I repeat, there was -- there were no members of the Croatian Army who would have crossed the border pursuant to an order, save for those who did it in that one exception, an exceptional case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last follow-up question, but we'll have an opportunity to return to this. You'll see I have a good memory, because I remember that you said that there were 13.000 volunteers. You said that earlier today. There were volunteers who, in fact, came from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had gone to Croatia, to return back to the ground. So I did take a very careful note of this. But for residents of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were they Croats, say, who were born in Zagreb but never been to Bosnia and Herzegovina, but declared themselves volunteers to join the HVO? Were there such cases, as far as you can see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very often. For example, in autumn 1992, from the battalion of the 2nd Guards Brigade that I was in command of in Sunja, lots of lads reported to me or contacted me offering me their help. I referred some of them to the BiH Army, asking them to help them with their experience, and I transferred them to the left bank of the Neretva to Mahala, and I gave some of them to the HVO. In the operation to liberate Capljina and fighting around Capljina, I had a few volunteers from Zagreb. There was some 15 of them. One of my volunteers was President Tudjman's grandson. In Capljina, there were volunteers who simply arrived from Croatia. And the 13.000, Your Honours, I believe that you remember the document that I provided to you, and when you said, Wow, that's a lot, was that as many as that, there is a cemetery in Zagreb, in Croatia, and you can see a list of all those Muslims who were killed as members of the Croatian Army, but those were not only people who resided in Croatia at the time, but also those who had arrived from Bosnia and Herzegovina when war in Croatia started, for various reasons that I would not be willing to discuss. For example, in the operation to defend Dubrovnik, during the last strike, when there was a question whether Dubrovnik would fall, we had a group of Herzegovinian volunteers who participated, and one of them got killed. And together with the citizens of Dubrovnik, they managed to save the city. I repeat, once again, it was a war not against the Serbs, irrespective of the territory or the republic, and there is no way you can do a vivisection as it could be done in a classical conflict of one state fighting another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just mentioned the example of President Tudjman's grandson, who was a volunteer. When people would learn that President Tudjman's grandson had volunteered, could they think or infer that, in fact, the entire Croatian Army had moved to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Could it be that some drew that kind of inference from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, President Tudjman's grandson was my soldier in Sunja also. He was a volunteer already in Sunja. He was under my command. He was an excellent fighter, an excellent lad, and he followed his commander down there. The interpretations of the war are various, to a large extent wrong, and if you don't have precise facts you cannot reconstruct anything. Facts are facts, very precise, as to what Croatia wanted, what it did, and how it behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Before we proceed, on page 53, line 9, I believe that the interpretation was good. However, it was mis-recorded. The way it was recorded, it seems that the General Praljak answered to Judge Antonetti's question that save for the unit consisting of 160 men in 1992, on the 10th of April, who had gone there to close the gap, and then in the record it says "in Heliodrom," and there should be another comma here after the gap that had to be closed, and then General Praljak moves on to a different area, which is Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no Heliodrom. It was a line which went from Citluk, Tepcici, Slipcici, towards Mostar, from Medjugorje towards the left, Tepcici and Slipcici towards Mostar. They didn't have anything whatsoever to do in Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there was a comma, the sentence would be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. General, you have just spoken about this, and now the next document is 3D03091. A reference is made to an officer of the Croatian Army that has been mentioned a lot of times in the courtroom. I believe that his name already rings a bell. Could you please explain who the officer is, and within the context of my questions could you take him as an example.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jasmin Jaganjac, whom I know very well, we cooperated quite a lot. He is a Muslim who joined the Croatian Army at the very beginning of the attack against Croatia, and I believe that for a while he was in charge of compiling a book of exercises and training for the Croatian Army because he had originated from the Yugoslav People's Army; and that's why I returned him to the unit called the Officers' Centre, as we had wanted to have in Mostar, where Muslims simply lagged behind, although they did wish to fight, but they were not well prepared. Pursuant to his wish and pursuant to our agreement, he was appointed the commander of the defence of Mostar after having been released from the Croatian Army. Mr. Jaganjac, together with me -- he was an official, and I was not officially appointed to be in charge of the operation in 1992, he was in charge of the liberation of the right bank of the Neretva River and the left bank of the Neretva River. After that, I returned to my regular tasks, and he remained down there until the moment -- and I don't know why. He wanted to return to his mother unit, which was the Officers' Centre. Around that time, Jasmin Jaganjac, after his return to the Officers' Centre, he became the military advisor of President Izetbegovic. At the time, we had achieved good military successes in the southern part, Petkovic, Stojic and all of us, and if I sometimes say "me," please do not think that one person can solve everything on his own in an army, because everything in fighting is resolved by all those who are fighting on the line. He remained an advisor of the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, up to the end of April 1993, and we had worked together for months in order to establish a joint command of the BiH Army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, when you started explaining the situation concerning Jasmin Jaganjac, well, I'd like to go back to that partially for the transcript and the speed you were speaking at, to make things quite clear, so I'd like to go back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Registrar, let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Counsel, sorry to interrupt you. Your Honours, for the record, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, in 1991, which army did this officer join in the defence against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jasmin Jaganjac joined the Croatian Army. Among other things, he worked in the Officers' Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just take it slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, he went voluntarily and became commander of the defence of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then, once again, according to his wishes, on the 22nd of October, he went back to his original unit and the Officers' Centre. Now, after that, I don't know the exact date but during that time, he also became a military advisor, the first military advisor to President Alija Izetbegovic, that is to say, the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what happened to his rights, as a member of the HV, when he went back or, rather, when he went away and came back? What happened to his rights? Were his -- once he activated his status in the HV, did he receive his rights again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kovacic, he enjoyed his rights all the time. He enjoyed his right to a salary. If he were wounded or killed, he would be treated as a Croatian soldier, so he retained all his rights. He left the Croatian Army to go to the HVO, to join the HVO and work together with them down there, and we'll see from the documents what it was he did in 1992, and then he returned to the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. Everything is quite clear now, crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like me. You can skip over the next documents. There's nothing to deal with there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. The -- although, on second thoughts, maybe not. Look at 3D02218 now, please. That's perhaps a characteristic document and tells us a great deal. It is dated the 14th of September, 1992. The document is 02218, signed by you, and addressed to the president of the republic. It says: "Dear Mr. President." What's this about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had a major problem, large numbers of refugees and soldiers who were in the Croatian Army but refugees at the same time, from Vukovar -- well, this was before Vukovar. But, anyway -- and the problem was a major one with the property belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army. The Yugoslav People's Army had enormous property, and a lot of property on the territory of the Republic of Croatia as well, so this property became the property of the state of Croatia, but the Ministry of Defence managed it, the MORH. Various town mayors came to me and asked to be given this or that plot of land, building or whatever, and there were very tense situations, because I had to explain to them that we, the MORH, managed that property, but that it was the state who was the owner and that it was the state who could decide whose property it would become. That was one problem. The other problem was that I wasn't very prone to have this property distributed in that kind of way, for the simple reason that they had no programme as to how they would utilise the land or property. They would be given a sizeable chunk and didn't know what they were going to do with that. And I asked them what the army was going to do. For example, if 100 hectares of land would be given to a town which had previously been owned and controlled by the Yugoslav People's Army, if they were to be given that free of charge without having a plan as to how they would utilise the property or land, well, that was a problem. That was one problem. The second problem was with respect to forcible entry into premises and buildings. You see, when people are expelled and houses set on fire, and these people fought, they expected that the many flats belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army would be assigned to them, and the government was dragging its feet with respect to that problem. And you know what my character is like. I tend to use strong words and strong language, but I insisted that they resolve the problem. And, If you don't resolve the problem legally, or even if you do, there will be problems, but if you don't solve it legally, then the problems are enormous. So that's what I talk about there and say that expulsions and other criminal activities continue to take place and the military police is expelling the HVO and civilians together in similar situations and so on. I'm writing the president, himself, directly and Mrs. Turic, who dealt with these problems. Anyway, the problem came to a head on the 15th of September, 1992, and this was a very sensitive question, and it began to infringe upon the authority of the state and the president and the government and the Assembly, because people were expelled from their homes, expelled from the army, and they just stormed the flats that were available. So this problem had to be solved urgently, and it was solved to a certain extent. And in the post-scriptum down at the bottom, I say that at the Coordination for Internal Policy meeting, the problem was resolved with the help of Mr. Milas.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, there was a technical mistake. It wasn't the HVO, it was the HV.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course, the HV. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 63, line 5 of the transcript. "The HVO" should read "the HV," and we can see that from the contents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I confirm that, the HV. And now the final sentence is that I was involved in the problem because for who knows what reason, they came to me to complain. Now, although other people were in charge of this, I was a sort of -- well, I was a sort of lightning rod, and the guys knew that if they brought a problem to me and I thought that it had -- should be solved, that then I would fight to have it solved. I wouldn't put it in a drawer and forget about it, and that I was ready to tackle any president or person in the government if I thought I was right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the next document, but I think you wanted to add something about the previous document. No? All right, then, let's move on to 3D02504. Is that an example of what you were telling us earlier on, that it's the easiest thing in the world to write an order and it's quite another matter to see whether it was implemented and whether it all functions properly? Is this an example of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. You need a lot of time for an organisation to be set up, especially an army, and that's something you can read in any textbook, even when there's no war on, let alone when there is a war. And here the Chief of Staff and I, myself, jointly signed this. It refers to the operative zones and all HV units, the Croatian Navy, Air Force, Commands of the HV and so on, and we list all the problems, from the IPD ranging to how regular reports are being sent out, when they should be sent out, any deviations, the homogeneity of the units, inter-human relations in the units, current issues, the reaction of the soldiers, and so on and so forth, rumours and the reasons for the soldiers' dissatisfaction. And then under D, part of the Psychological Department -- or, rather, some of what the IPD did was to work to look into the combat readiness of the troops. And under D we see that in some units the soldiers' readiness was at a lower level, morale was low, and that it was the commanders whose fault it was, that there was very poor commanding, that there was fatigue among the units, that the units were being deployed and utilised without the necessary preparations beforehand, that there was a lack of direct contact with the soldiers, and so on and so forth. And I'll be happy to answer any queries from Their Honours, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I've got a question, actually, because the document, at least the translation that I'm looking at, does not appear to bear a date in the heading or at the bottom of the document, although in the body, about midway through the first page, there's a reference to a report that has to be delivered before the 24th of July, 1992. So I wonder if the general could give us the time-frame for this or indicate whether this document is dated sometime prior to the 24th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is quite certainly July 1992, the 7th of July, in fact -- or, rather, July, it's July 1992. I don't know what day it was. Probably a day or two before. If I gave them a dead-line of 48 hours to report back to me, then it might have been the 22nd of July and 48 hours would have been a dead-line I would have set.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On page 64, line 23, it says "HVO," and it should read "HV." It says "HVO units" instead of "HV units."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next document is similar in content, 3D02859, of the 25th of March, 1992, once again signed by you. It contains two reports as attachments. Could you explain this, because it's fairly typical.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're dealing with the 25th of March, 1992, once I had been appointed assistant minister, and I enumerate all the points: demobilisation, which is a major problem, who should be demobilised, who wishes to stay on and so on; then promotions and transfers, "transfers" meaning that all people who came from the Yugoslav People's Army were promised the same rank as they held while in the JNA, generals remained generals, although there were certain misunderstandings because the guys thought that some of the ranks were too high and that they would have to prove their mettle on the battle-front before they were allowed to carry the same rank. Then we had the problem of officers and soldiers' training, which was supposed to begin straight away. Then there was the consideration of commendations and decorations and so on, and I state that difficulties emerged with respect to legal regulations. Now, who this was addressed to, I don't really know. Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't see from this, but I'd like to draw your attention to the report attached, especially the first one dated the 24th of March. After sizing up the situation on the ground, certain irregularities were uncovered. Can this all be considered as part and parcel of the building up of an army, discipline and order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the most important thing here is -- or I want it to be understood in the following way: that we never wanted to hide anything. All the bad points, all the storming of flats, the problems, and a document we forgot to present, suicides, killings, legal proceedings against people, military courts and so on, I state here and now that the documents that we compiled and so on, we never hid any problems. All this was accessible to all the journalists, military attaches. They could go into the field to see what the problems were. We just tried to use our knowledge and experience to help solve the problems, but we never did anything to hide them, any evil-doing. Everything was recorded. People were taken to task. If the perpetrators were apprehended, they would be taken to court. They weren't swept under the carpet. Nothing was hidden from the public or any observer from the international community. And as you were able to see, when I was in Herceg-Bosnia, for example, every journalist had the right to go and see for themselves when they wanted to, what they wanted to see, and I say that with absolute certainty because that is something that I okayed and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, what you've just told us, was that a pattern of behaviour? Is that how you behaved later on in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm too old to change my feathers. I think from start to finish, I always acted in the same way, identically. I didn't change one iota.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I'd like to move on to a different topic now, but I think that it's time for our break, or at least it is in a minute or two. So shall we take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it might be better to have a break now, since you're going to move on to another topic. Let's break for 20 minutes until 10 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, as we said yesterday, just briefly, and I'll repeat it for everybody and for the Trial Chamber here, you mentioned that, amongst other things that you did in your department, the department was in charge of publishing "The Croatian Soldier" magazine that was in the Defence Ministry of Croatia, and from that magazine we can see the positions of the Croatian government and most prominent figures of the Croatian politics. We're going to look at the magazine now, and when we come to each of the pages, I would kindly ask you to read the e-court number at the bottom for the interpreters and for everybody else's benefit. This also has a bearing on the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and can you please look at 3D01278. The date is 15 January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay, 279, yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Croatian Soldier" was the magazine of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. I have the originals, of course, if anybody wants to look at the originals. Maybe the Trial Chamber would like to see the magazine to see its design. "The Croatian Soldier" summarises all the problems that were present in Croatia with regard to the Croatian Army, the positions of the Ministry of Defence, the positions of the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and in a certain way they are a succinct representation of political and military positions, desires, problems, intentions, everything that was going on at the time. The date here is the 15th of January, 1993, describing the meeting of the editors-in-chief of Croatian journals and newspapers with General Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, just a moment. This is 3D29-0512?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. And in the second paragraph here, the president says that in 1992, the Croatian area established itself as the factor of peace in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and the international factors are counting with it, and they are interested in the issue of the Croatian official policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in light of the fact that some individuals from some of the states had voiced some accusations which were not justified. And the president briefly speaks about the threats that exist in his view. He also speaks about the Mujahedin and the willingness of some Islamic states to help them. And in the last part on the right-hand side, he says that no sanctions were imposed upon Croatia; every attempt to do so has failed. There are statements by the Islamic states that Croatia is the only state in Europe that had recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina and received over half a million refugees. There is a resolution of the United Nations to that effect. And then he says that the Croatian politicians were very much interested in Bosnia and Herzegovina because the development of events in Bosnia-Herzegovina very largely influenced the territory of Southern Croatia from Split to Dubrovnik just the way I described it in my testimony. Croatian politicians did take into account the interests of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he continues to say that because of that, Bosnia-Herzegovina is today not a part of the Greater Serbia. Croatia has enabled the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina to organise themselves and to defend themselves. And to make sure that Bosnia-Herzegovina was not annexed to the Greater Serbia, Croatia advocated the referendum for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina as a community of three constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, I have to interrupt you. We have a wrong document on e-court. I need 3D01278, and the page number is 3D29-051.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have the right document. And, finally, it says that the president emphasised, and this has to be underlined, that Croatia itself, and Muslims themselves, cannot militarily end the war, especially not in their favour, because of the supremacy of the Yugoslav People's Army. If the war continues, this would lead to further complications in European and global terms. The international factors have adopted a political solution which is in keeping with the real position and the democratic relationships in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Franjo Tudjman did not want a war. He tried to see that things were resolved in a peaceful way, as much as he could. The following document, 3D29-0513. I'm just going to read the title, "To the Best Western Military Academies," which means that classes started for high-ranking officers at the Officers' Centre. People had to be educated subsequently, post festum, unfortunately. However, it arises from all the documents, all the positions that were voiced, that our best officers would attend Western academies, and that the overall desire of the Croatian Army and the Republic of Croatia was for Croatia to be integrated into NATO and the European Union. So much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The following --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The following document is 3D01279. The issue covers the period from 19 to 28 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading. The page number is 3D29-0515. Autumn 1992, Croatia started systematically recruiting conscripts for regular military service. In the second paragraph, you can see that there was a 95 per cent response of the recruits. Those who could not serve in the army were to be provided different jobs and posts in the civilian life. And it says that every recruit, irrespective of the evaluation of the recruiting commission, can file an appeal against their decision within two weeks. And in the second paragraph, in the right-hand-side column, it says that there were no requests for the civilian service in the army, although every recruit was entitled to file such a request. Every soldier had the right to opt for the civilian service in the army, rather than taking a weapon in their hands. Finally, it says that we have established five training centres where the military training will take place. So much about that. And now we are moving on to 3D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have again a question. What has this got to do with our case? Recruitment in Croatia, the fact that Croatians can opt out of being recruited, that there is an appeal, what is the relationship to our case? I do not even see a fathom that leads to something like joint criminal enterprise, let alone all the rest. I am a bit afraid, when I see this huge file, that we are expected to listen to a lot of evidence that I cannot find the link, but I stand to be corrected. If I am convinced, that's so much the better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, Franjo Tudjman is the first one on the list of people charged with the joint criminal enterprise, an intention regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina, a nationalist, and so on and so forth. There are a lot of accusations against Franjo Tudjman. Now I believe that it is necessary, and finally it will maybe take no more than two hours in this trial, it is necessary to show that the first accused on the list of those who were charged with joint criminal enterprise with regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and according to the accusations that we heard about nationalism and other things, I believe that we should look at the overall way of thinking or the way the Republic of Croatia was established and how it developed. It is necessary to show that from the very outset, there was an intention and desire in the state to introduce the best principles of what we call the Western civilised world, and I believe that even if we spend two hours on the things that are not directly tied to the indictment, we'll provide you with a picture of the world of the actors who are charged with crimes here, and I'm talking about Susak, Tudjman and Bobetko. And in these texts, you will see how they developed the army, what -- the problems they had to face. And even if we -- if we don't see what problems they faced, it will turn out that everything was easy and could have been resolved just like that. There may be things that I can skip. I don't know which ones they are. I just wanted to demonstrate what all of us did, how we did what we did, how hard we worked, what problems we faced, what were our intentions, our desires, and what kind and how much effort we invested in order to achieve all that. This would be by way of explanation to your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because of the joint criminal enterprise, I do wish to be heard and make a record as well, because I think that -- and I heard what General Praljak said, but I think it must be understood that while we're dealing with Bosnia-Herzegovina, you know, Croatia is -- essentially has been charged with joint criminal enterprise, and we have to understand the situation as it existed at the time. Croatia was occupied, was fighting its war. Croatia wants recognition. It received recognition, but it wants its territory back, it wants assistance. Here we have -- and what the general is trying to show is that Croatia has its own problems. It's trying to resolve those problems in a lawful, legitimate manner, and at the same time it is working with and cooperating with the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina because ultimately they will face some of the same problems. This is part and parcel of this joint criminal enterprise. I can understand the Court's frustration, especially when we go into this sort of minute detail. However, again, if we're going to be talking about equality of arms, if I can put it in those terms, the Trial Chamber sat here and allowed Dr. Miller, a professor from the United States who probably has never visited Bosnia-Herzegovina, to talk about 1996, 1997, 1998, 2000 BiH, which is not part of the indictment, and sat there and said, Well, this is interesting information. Let's listen to it because it's part and parcel of the joint criminal enterprise. Here now we have General Praljak, who's talking about Croatia, who is a member -- which is a member of the joint criminal enterprise, as alleged. That's the problem. The problem is that you've allowed this indictment to be so over-broad that we have a responsibility to defend everything. And one last thing, if I may add, Your Honours. With the last witness of the Stojic Defence, there was an interesting commentary that came from one of the members of the Bench, which is to say, well, we, the Defence, have not countered that, and therefore the Trial Chamber was accepting this -- accepting the Prosecution's position. It had to do with the map and the borders and what have you, that we haven't provided a map with the actual borders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which we maintain did not have borders because it was a community and in some municipalities it was just -- they were just in areas. Nonetheless, from that -- from that little inkling, what I got was a few nights of no sleep, thinking, okay, I understand now that at least in some Judges' minds, I have to prove the case, I have to prove what the Prosecution is putting forward, I have to prove against whatever it is, because if they say it, then somehow it's being accepted as the Gospel. I know I'm overstretching it, but that's how we see it. So now we're forced to go into all this minute detail, but because of the length and breadth and depth of this indictment, because if we don't, we may see then later saying, Well, you didn't challenge it; therefore, it must be. That's part of the problem. I mean, I'm not pointing fingers at anybody, but it's a sort of this overwhelming fear on our part that if we don't challenge everything -- and I understand the Prosecution recently has filed a motion which we are going to be responding to, that if they don't address something that General Praljak addresses, the Trial Chamber is not to take that as an acquiescence that they're accepting that, and I think that's a legitimate way of looking at it. Just because somebody says something and the other side doesn't challenge it doesn't mean that the Trial Chamber automatically accept it. The Trial Chamber will decide what weight, if any, to give to it. But when we hear comments from the Bench saying, Well, you haven't challenged this; therefore, it's -- you know, the Prosecution has proved the point, and we haven't gone through all of the evidence, that's how we're perceiving it, we're forced to be in a position where we have to challenge every minute little detail, which is why it's going to take four years to try this case. So perhaps they could speed it up, perhaps it would even be better if there were some transitional statements as far as focusing what is relevant so that everybody can follow it. Some of us kind of understand that, but from the Bench I understand it may be a little bit difficult. So my colleague could perhaps give the reasoning to the Trial Chamber as to why -- you know, with a transitional statement, and then General Praljak adding the commentary, it may be a little bit easier to follow and it won't be as frustrating, but I do understand the Court's frustration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, we're not going to embark on such problems. I do not think that the intention of my fellow Judge was to develop a whole controversy or a debate on the joint criminal enterprise. Mr. Karnavas has said things, but he had said them before, so nothing new. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to say something not only for the record, but I also believe that it will contribute to the clarification of the situation. I understand Judge Trechsel's remark, and I must admit that this was my initial thought when I received the set of documents containing the issues of "The Croatian Soldier." However, after having read the set of documents prepared by General Praljak, it became clear to me why are these documents important and significant for this case, and primarily for the case of the joint criminal enterprise. In "The Croatian Soldier," there is an analysis by a prominent Croatian geo-strategic analyst which says that a military intervention would be desirable on the part of the international community because it would lead to the solution of the problem of the Serb aggression. I believe that this points very clearly to the fact that there are no pretensions against the territory of a different state, because if those were the pretensions or aspirations, then nobody would have wanted the foreign soldiers to come to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. Furthermore, there is another text by a prominent analyst/journalist -- just one more word, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you're not testifying. What you are saying you may express as part of your cross-examination, but now you are developing an entire theory, which is equivalent to testimony. I think it's better to ask Mr. Praljak a question, and he will provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might I just point out another piece of text that unambiguously shows that Bosnia-Herzegovina, in -- within the AVNOJ boundaries, was not challenged at all, but that the internal order and setup of the state was the question, and they are topics that are important as far as the JCE is concerned, and perhaps the Defence of General Praljak could continue analysing "The Croatian Soldier" editions and I think it will make things clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I can see Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll be very brief. I'm not going to make anything that sounds like a closing argument. Last week I -- at one point I rose and indicated that the Prosecution considered certain testimony to be irrelevant. However, I indicated that I was going to be very reluctant to continue to object on that grounds. I know there are some -- they're differing views as to the amount of latitude that the Trial Chamber may wish to give the general in giving his evidence, because not only is he a witness, but he's also an accused, and so there's the matter of the testimony. And the Prosecution, I think, is at this point less likely to object on relevancy grounds, even if we have our own reservations about that, because of that and because, frankly, it tends ultimately to just result in a lot of time being wasted. Now, there is a separate issue which relates to the documents and the exhibits, and again just to save time and so the record is clear, the Prosecution's not going to stand up and object to every document that we might submit is irrelevant. However, just so everyone knows, we intend to reserve our right to object to documents that are tendered by the Praljak Defence in the future when the documents themselves are tendered as part of their IC lists. So we're trying to just stay seated, not raise too many objections, in order to keep things moving, and reserve our objections to documents until the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, I do not intend to take up much time, but I want to react briefly to what Mr. Karnavas has said to say that basically I'm in full agreement. I accept practically everything you have put forward, no objection. My only -- where I probably depart a bit from you is that I think this is really very far off, and principally there can be no question that Croatia is accused here, at least formally definitely not. Mr. Tudjman is not accused. They are mentioned as members of JCE, but they are not accused here. And I think that if you think that a state -- a certain policy of a state is put into question, which I admit is the case here, it's not necessarily very effective, in my view, to contradict this by showing that many things were okay, because that's not contested. No one says everything was wrong in Croatia. No one says Croatia was not a state intent on realising true democracy on respecting the rule of law. So to the extent that evidence just tends to prove this, it, in a way, fits the void because there is no obstacle, no one is saying the contrary. That was what prompted me to make the observation I made. I hope that we are basically in agreement, though we do not necessarily have to agree in the detail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, when I have a document in front of me, I look at it and I try to ask questions which shed light on the issues at hand. In the document in front of us, there is a detail which may actually be important, in particular in the light of the case law of the Appeals Chamber, in the Kordic/Cerkez case, which recognised that the Republic of Croatia had control over the HVO. So when I ask a question, there's always a legal background to it, and I try to look at the future. Now, in the document in front of us, it is said that the conscripts, 95 per cent of them, have a military booklet, a new military booklet. This is in the last line of the English version of the document. Let's focus on this military booklet for a second. Let's take the example of the grandson of late Mr. Tudjman. He's, first of all, a conscript, and then he's incorporated in a Croatian unit. Therefore, I assume that in his military booklet his date of conscription will be indicated. But if he has a military booklet and then later on he says, I'm going as a volunteer to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what will his military booklet indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, we're talking about August 1992, when the first soldiers were being taken in, and they were to do eight-month stints before they -- for instance, President Tudjman's grandson was a volunteer, like I was. He came to Sunja of his own free will. He didn't have a booklet of this kind. He came of his own free will, and went to Capljina of his own free will and returned. So this is the beginning of the recruitment of the new soldiers, the recruits. And let me also tell you that it was only in Operation Storm that they took part in the war operations, because in the meantime they didn't need to because the functions of defence along the separation lines with the rebel Serbs was something that professional brigades were engaged in, or, rather, those volunteers who were in the Croatian Army and were still salaried in the Croatian Army. So Tudjman's grandson had nothing to do with any military booklet of this kind. I never had a military booklet, myself. So it was just the first recruitment of these young people who spent eight or ten months in the army later on; ten months, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have not answered my question. Let me go back to this topic. Let's take the example of a conscript. The 28th of August, 1992, and he's doing his eight-month stint, and then he is assigned to the 124th Brigade of the Croatian Army, for example. In April 1993 or thereabouts, or in July - it doesn't matter - this soldier says, I'd like to join General Praljak, who is now an HVO commander. We're talking about July. He therefore informs his Command that he's leaving. What I want to know is as follows: What will his military booklet indicate? Because, of course, this is not an entirely innocent question. It has a legal basis. I'm inquiring about the issue of overall control, so please provide a specific answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, I'm giving a specific answer to the best of my knowledge. I can't answer your question beyond that, because I don't know that of the people who arrived, anybody had a booklet of this kind, so I said exactly what I know. A volunteer, or volunteers, received a piece of paper saying that he could go, and we called it the Southern Front. So he would go to the Southern Front, and that is cover for him if he were to be killed or whatever. That's what I know, that's the extent of my knowledge. I can't answer your question otherwise, because I've never seen a booklet like this before, nor do I know what kind of entries were made, nor do I know that any of the people who had done their military service were ascribed to a brigade. The brigades were filled with those volunteers who were there before, right up to Operations Flash and Storm, and the problem was demobilisation because many more people wanted to be in the Croatian Army as volunteers than we were able to cater for at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask you a follow-up question, under the control of your lawyer, who also pleaded in the Kordic/Cerkez case and therefore who knows this case very well. We've heard evidence according which HV soldiers were found dead. They were found with a military ID or a military booklet. This is evidence from the Kordic case. Of course, I do not have these military booklets in front of me. This HV soldier died during the fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a volunteer, from what you said. This soldier had a military booklet. What was in his military booklet to show -- to demonstrate that he was not an HV member anymore but that he was with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, he would never have that entry. He could have carried, but not a booklet like that, but something smaller. This document, he would carry that document, and if he were killed as a volunteer, that booklet would be found, but it would never say: "Sent to the HVO, to Bosnia-Herzegovina." Nobody could make an entry like that, but they would carry this with them, and what was recognised was the right of a Croatian soldier, either to be buried if he was killed, or regards his pension, if he was wounded he go to -- be sent to hospital and they would admit him like anybody else, but not the right to send him there. Nobody had that right and nobody could write that down. Nobody could say, You're going to Bosnia-Herzegovina to fight on the BH Army side or the HVO side. And the officers of the BH Army, well, we would receive requests from Rijeka for so many people and so on, allow them to go to the BH Army. That was okayed. They were given permission to go, and they retained their rights. But then they left and came back, but it never said -- there was no entry to say they were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, just as if they hadn't moved out, moved away, as far as their rights were concerned, that is. It's as if they had gone nowhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's been recorded in the transcript. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, let me help you out. I know that you had no reason to look at the military booklets, but perhaps to make things clear, I think that we're talking about two concepts here; the ID card and the military booklet in which somebody's training is recorded, years of service or whatever. That other one is a book, a booklet, with several pages, and it is a register -- recorded in the register. But this is just an ID card, but it's a military ID card; right? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a military ID card, identification card.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. There are no columns there to be filled in. It looks like an ordinary ID card; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a small ID card, no columns where you can make any entries. And when I completed my service in 1995 and 1996, and when I went to the Military Department, I received my little booklet. That's the first time I saw that they existed, because I was still a conscript, and this is what they wrote in there. That's an illustration of bureaucracy. It said: "Colonel General Slobodan Praljak, Croatian Army, incapable -- not capable for the army." So upon completion of the war, a month later it says there: "Colonel General, unfit for military service -- Colonel General Slobodan Praljak unfit for military service."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you mentioned the soldier in Kordic and Cerkez, Your Honour. That is an identification document, and that's the only HVO ID document he had, because nobody issued him with anything else. But of course we can't testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my room, I have the ID document of the Croatian Army, and I have the ID of the HVO, and also the ID of the BH Army, because I received that ID document too. Arif Pasalic provided me with one of those, this ID card saying that I was a member of the BH Army. And I'll show that, of course, I'll bring it into court. I can bring it in tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, this BH Army booklet is on our list of exhibits, and we'll show it in due course, but we didn't consider it necessary to show the HV one because it's a notorious fact, so notorious facts need not be demonstrated. Although we can show you, for purposes of demonstration, we can bring in that ID card. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, General Praljak, I propose that you continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll skip over -- well, actually, Judge Trechsel, it is a fact that there are certain things which are there more -- which perhaps you would not have put there, and that's out of an over-abundance of caution, because I was afraid that I wouldn't be explaining it properly if I didn't include all these things. Now, if you say, Praljak, it's not relevant, and throw it out, I might have done that. But as I say, I claim that there are highly relevant portions there. I'll go and look at 3D290517 now, which shows that civilian protection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like this to be recorded, to follow up on the intervention of my fellow Judge on the joint criminal enterprise. Indeed, Mr. Tudjman is not an accused because he's dead, so he can't be here, but were he alive, he would be here, he would be accused. General Bobetko, were he alive, would also be an accused. I wanted the record to be straight on this, and this has to be kept in mind when addressing the issue of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here that Civilian Protection took part in taking care of 900.000 refugees and displaced persons, and in the penultimate paragraph it says that it should be stressed that the implementation of these tasks, especially when it comes to the evacuation of the population from areas in jeopardy, was impossible without coordination and assistance from the Croatian Army units, Slavonski Brod, Pozega and so on. And I just wish to stress that 900.000 refugees, and the Croatian Army did a great deal, is, of course, an enormous number for such a small country, making up almost a quarter of the population or 20 per cent of the entire population. Now let's skip over the next document. 3D290518 is next. Once again, it says that the Croatian Army education and training will be compatible to what it is in the West, that there will be no special military academies, but that there will be faculties, and that they will go to civilian universities and faculties. And then we can skip over the exchange of prisoners, prisoner exchange. And can we look at 3D29-521 and 522, where it says that a war in the neighbouring country has shown to the world that what Croatia experienced in recent years, due to regional security, it is necessary to -- well, it refers to Serb nationalism and refers to a neighbouring country, that is to say, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. A merely technical matter. Would it not be possible to refer to the pages at the bottom of the page, because when you give the number, 3D361553, that style, you give it in the B/C/S version, and then we first try to find it there to see what it could refer to, and then we switch to the English text, and we've almost found it when you come to the next page, and we have to start this again. So it would really be helpful if there were a possibility to ease this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This article now, Your Honour, is e-court 3D361544, and the Croatian number is 3D01279, and the page number on e-court is 3D29-0521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And it is still in the document 3D01279 and not in 3D01280, which had already been called. That's why I was a bit lost. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Journalist Davor Gjenero is one of those civilian journalists who dealt with the topic. On the following page, I would like to show, for example, a visit by the French president, Francois Mitterand, who was on the way to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next page is 3D29-0522, and in the English version it is the next page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry to say in the presence of His Honour Judge Antonetti, but Francois Mitterand was more than inclined to support the Serbs, and it says here that en route to Sarajevo he landed at Split, as if the country he landed in was unknown. He proceeded towards Sarajevo, and there he offered the Serbs a get-away, although Croatia had already been recognised by many states including France. These are simple illustrations to show what games were being played. I'm not accusing anybody. However, I would like to say that the world had its own geo-strategic interests, and within those frameworks, we had to swim the best we could, and it wasn't easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, maybe just a couple of words. You know the journalist Mr. Davor Gjenero?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gjenero, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was he just a simple journalist or was he more than just a journalist?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a political and military analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is he still present in the Croatian general public?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you consider him a qualified person, as a military and political analyst?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a military and political analyst, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then the article goes on to speak about the CNN turnaround, when the first transport aircraft flew over Zagreb and Split and started transporting humanitarian aid to Sarajevo. They started applying for permission from the Croatian government, which had not always been the case. People did what they will, almost. Although the corridors had gone through Croatia at that time, nobody really minded us, whether they could land, what they were carrying, where they were carrying their cargo, which all -- and now I would like to ask for the next document, 3D29-0523. It's the same document. Actually, the next page is 3D29-0523.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the document referring to the French president who went to Sarajevo, the French president landed in Split, but when? On what date, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in 1992, sometime in autumn 1992. I wouldn't be able to give you the exact date. In any case, it was in 1992. Namely, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, some states already showed a desire to stop the Serb aggression against Sarajevo and to shell the Serb positions instead. According to all foreign and domestic analysts, Francois Mitterand, where he landed in Sarajevo, put a halt to any such plans and provided the Serbs with another chance to do whatever. According to what I know, what was published, he said to Alija Izetbegovic, The West will not intervene, the Serbs will not be bombed, and you, sir, get together with Karadzic and talk to him. As far as I know, Izetbegovic tried to ask Mitterand, How I'm going to talk to Karadzic if he wants to kill me at the same time? And that's how the conversation between the two ended, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, there's something I didn't understand. Did he land in Split or in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First Split and then Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At the fall of 1992, the Republic of Croatia was recognised internationally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was after the date when the moratorium expired by which the European community asked from Croatia to put a moratorium on its recognition. Maybe it was even later. I can't tell you whether it was in 1992 or the beginning of 1993. In any case -- just a moment. If you can bear with me, I may be able to find it in the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there was air control? Was there air control? When a plane lands, there should have been permission asked and there should have been a flight plan, so in fact the Republic of Croatia was informed of the fact that a personality was about to land in Split? Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a traffic -- air traffic control, and the plane landed in Split. I don't know whether they had been told who was on board the plane. Maybe they didn't, for security reasons. I know that the Croatian government was hurt by the fact that President Mitterand never said to his counterpart, the Croatian president, President, I've landed in Split, en route to Sarajevo. I believe that everybody was hurt and nothing to that effect happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand better. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I may have missed something, so excuse me if it's a repetition. Mr. Praljak, who is the editor of "Hrvatski Vojnik"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the longest period of time, the editor was Mr. Ivan Tolj. He ended the war as a general in the Croatian Army, but before the war he was a writer and a poet. He had nothing whatsoever to do with the military before the war. He was a writer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And during the war, was he in your department? Was he integrated in the fraction of the leadership of the army that you, yourself, headed as an assistant minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we kept him within our part, although he was an independent department and an independent editorial board. However, we maintained constant consultations about all the matters, such as technical and financial matters. He belonged to the part that I was in charge of, but when it comes to the texts they published, they were independent, they could publish whatever they wanted after consultations with President Tudjman and myself. Along the general lines, there was a general editorial policy, and within that every journalist was responsible for their own writing, so -- except for the facts that I mentioned, which was -- were the armament, the modern aircraft, the education of the army, which cannot be found in here. I'm talking about purely technical and military matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to assist everybody and put things in a temporal context, my learned friends have just helped me and told me that the French president landed on the 29th of June, 1992. That's when he landed in Split, and from there he took a helicopter to fly to Sarajevo. I'm not testifying, I'm not trying to testify. I'm just trying to put things in a context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We are now at 3D1279, and the page is 3D290523, and the English translation is on e-court page 3D361547.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Honours, I will not go into great length with regard to this text. First of all, I would like to explain here you can see "Herceg-Bosna." A lot of analysts don't think that this is the same Herceg-Bosna that we keep on mentioning here at the court. This is what Bosnia and Herzegovina is referred to -- this is one of its historical names. A lot of Croats and historians called this state the way it was called in many historical books, which is "Herceg-Bosna," so this is not the Herceg-Bosna that appears in the indictment. It is actually tantamount to Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the first thing. The second thing I would like to say is Mr. Vlatko Cvrtila is the best military analyst and sociologist of war in Croatia to my mind, to what I know. And here, as you can see in this text, he simply analyses what should be done, what are European dilemmas, what is the Serbian trap, what is the game played by the intelligence services, how many soldiers should be sent by the international community in order to bring peace to Bosnia. This is an excellent analytical text. In one place, it says that according to the "Newsweek" research, an intervention was -- Bosnia and Herzegovina is supported by 53 per cent of the interviewees. What follows is an explanation about the dilemmas of the international community, and it is abundantly clear that Croatia was extremely interested in somebody's intervention. To be honest, we were waiting for an intervention, like the sun to come out. We wanted somebody to help us and place soldiers on the borders between Croatia and Serbia, and Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and force --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I would like to interrupt you for just one minute. We are now drawing to the end of today's sitting. I really -- I'm not quite sure if I may agree to you. According to my own background, knowing about Herceg-Bosna, when you said previously, it was in line 50 -- the 15th, that "Herceg-Bosna" also could have also meant the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as I do recall "Herceg-Bosna" has been mainly used for that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is actually Herzegovina, if I'm not mistaken, and it is what I learned as a Hungarian before also concerning the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its annexation -- occupation and annexation. But it is, of course, a question of fact, and I am ready to accept anything which is being proved. And frankly, it doesn't prejudge the indictment, but I just wanted to tell you this one. And probably we may go on with this issue without any further kind of controversy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may -- just one second. Not trying to add any controversy, but we did present evidence through one of our witnesses - I believe it was Borislav Puljic - who brought with him a book which was authored by a Muslim - Bosniak by today - pre-dating the events, and the title of it was "Herceg-Bosna." So obviously the term has some historical context. That's all I wanted to add, and that is in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prandler, what is referred to in the indictment is Herceg-Bosna, the way it is implied, but it is certain that there is, in history books, because the ruler of Bosnia was Herceg, that was his title. That was a nobleman who governed Bosnia and had been appointed by Austro-Hungarian empire. In many history books, that area is seen as comprising of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the total territory. This is still used currently, to my great dismay, and Herceg-Bosnia. And in this text, "Herceg-Bosna" is just another name for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and here a reference is made to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As such, there is a number of history books in which "Bosnia-Herzegovina" is tantamount to "Herceg-Bosna" as a geographical term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for this explanation. As a matter of fact, the very word "Herceg," H-e-r-c-e-g, is a Hungarian word coming, of course, from German "Herzog," written with a Z in the middle. But, anyway, it is up to the historians. I stand to be convinced and corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, we have five more minutes. Maybe you could single out one or two of the most interesting ideas from this article.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this is interesting. Looking at the text, which is an analysis, it's very difficult to single out anything in particular. I'm saying that everything is interesting. And let's finish just one more text from "The Croatian Soldier," which is 3D29-0527. Again, "Herceg-Bosna" is tantamount to "Bosnia," and it says if you don't know the history of the three communities that constitute Bosnia, you will not be able to understand the developments that are taking place at the moment. Gjenero again gives a summary, historical summary, to tell us what should be understood from the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to understand the tragic events that took place in 1992. He mentions Benjamin Kalaj, who was the minister of finance, who held Bosnia under his immediate control, and Benjamin Kalaj was a Hungarian --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we get a reference to the English page there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just going to read it. 3D361553 is the reference you were asking for. 1553.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally Davor Gjenero says that the Serbs are doing their best to prevent any possibility of a life with or along with the other two ethnic communities. The ethnic cleansing of the territory is thus being presented as a solution and simplification of the complex situation. The Croatian national community so far didn't do a single thing to demonstrate a lack of loyalty to the Bosnian and Herzegovinian state, and the Croatian Defence Council, in the territory where Croats constitute a respectable number, has efficiently resisted all the aggressor attempts and onslaughts. The Croatian Community is not trying to use the war situation to impose the political solution for the future political organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Instead, it is being cooperative and participates in the negotiations under the auspices of the European community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 3D290528, and in the English version it is 3D361554 and continues on to 55, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
